figures.caption: Schematic illustration of deep dynamic compaction
figures.description: Description Choosing between impact (DDC) and vibration (VC) densification of loose cohesionless soils. DDC tamper 10 to 40 kips dropped 30 to 100 ft; depth of improvement generally 10 to 35 ft (p. 4-1). An ironing pass (low-level energy on a tight grid) compacts the surface left loose to crater depth. Deep compaction is most applicable to loose cohesionless soils with little to no fines. Most vibro-compaction is done by the wet (water jetting) method (p. 4-3). VC outcome depends on in situ soil type and gradation, point spacing, equipment, and compaction duration.

figures.caption: SPT liquefaction chart for magnitude 7.5 earthquakes
figures.description: Liquefaction Potential and Mitigation Assessment Setting densification targets for DDC or VC to mitigate earthquake liquefaction. Treat to the bottom of the liquefiable layer and laterally a distance equal to the treatment depth (Cooke and Mitchell 1999) (p. 4-8). For embankments, treating between crest and toe is more effective against lateral deformation. Example: (N1)60 = 10 with CSR = 0.25 liquefies unless (N1)60 is raised above 22 blows/ft (p. 4-10). Usual design: factor of safety CRR/CSR greater than 1.5, minimum 1.3 (p. 4-10). Several closely grouped low values are more significant than a few scattered ones (p. 4-11).

figures.caption: Phase diagram model of soil behavior during deep dynamic compaction
figures.description: Densification of Loose Deposits Densifying loose granular soils and fills with DDC. Works best on dry granular materials and saturated, free-draining soils (p. 4-14). Saturated sands liquefy under DDC and end denser, less susceptible to liquefaction (p. 4-15). Fine-grained soils: best below the plastic limit; generally not recommended for PI > 8 with high saturation (p. 4-15). Figure 4-4: each phase expels gas and liquid, lowering the void ratio; solids unchanged (pp. 4-15 to 4-16).

figures.caption: Grouping of soils for deep dynamic compaction
figures.description: Geotechnical Classifying a deposit's suitability for DDC from gradation, saturation and permeability. Zone 1 (pervious): k generally greater than 10^-5 m/s; best suited; works partially or fully saturated (p. 4-21). Zone 2 (intermediate): k generally 10^-5 to 10^-8 m/s; works with energy in multiple phases (p. 4-22). Zone 3 (impervious clayey): k generally less than 10^-8 m/s; not recommended if saturated; partially saturated clay fills at or below the plastic limit have improved (p. 4-21). Field permeability, not grain size gradation, dictates suitability (p. 4-22). Test sections with SPT, CPT or PMT before and after energy are valuable where stratigraphy varies.

figures.description: Design Overview Applies to choosing the design method for MSE and GRS walls and abutments. Simplified Method: reinforcement as tension inclusions; LRFD per AASHTO (2014) and GEC 11. Coherent Gravity Method permitted for steel reinforced walls. figures.caption: Reinforced slope applications
figures.description: Applications Use to identify where reinforced soil slopes fit highway projects. Steepened slopes on firm foundations; road widening within ROW. Slope repair reusing slide debris. Also bridge span reduction, detours, sloughing prevention, wet fine-grained fills, levees.

figures.caption: RSS face geometries - smooth, wrapped, and stepped
figures.description: RSS Facing Use when selecting and detailing the facing of a reinforced soil slope. Face wrap may be unnecessary for slopes up to about 1H:1V. Reinforcement spacing for wrapped or unwrapped faces: no greater than 16 in. Hard faced systems: maximum spacing generally 32 in. or the facing width. Facings are soft (vegetated) or hard; wraps confine the face.

figures.caption: Failure modes for reinforced soil slope
figures.description: Design Overview Applies to the design basis and failure modes of reinforced soil slopes. Limit equilibrium, allowable stress design; LRFD not developed for slopes. Failure modes: internal, external, compound. Optimized layouts can give nearly equal factors of safety in all modes (Berg et al. 1989).

figures.caption: Flow chart of steps for reinforced soil slope design
figures.description: Design Steps Applies to the design sequence for reinforced soil slopes on firm foundations. Design steps shown as a flow chart (Figure 10-12) for RSS on firm foundations. Detailed steps and examples: GEC 11.

figures.caption: Typical soil nail wall construction sequence
figures.description: Construction Applies to the field construction sequence of drilled and grouted soil nail walls. Excavation lift 2.5 to 7 ft, typically 3 to 5 ft; must stand one to two days. Initial facing: lightly reinforced 4-in. shotcrete; nut tightened within 24 h. Shotcrete 3-day strength before next lift; plan on 72 h cure. WWM panels overlap at least one full mesh cell.

figures.caption: Main components of a solid bar soil nail and wall facing
figures.description: Materials Use when specifying soil nail tendons, hardware, grout, corrosion protection, facing and drainage. Components of a solid bar soil nail and facing (Figure 10-14) (p. 10-67).

figures.caption: Deep patch roadway embankment repair
figures.description: Deep Patching Applies to temporary repair of chronically sliding roadway fills in steep terrain. Temporary repair; slows rather than arrests movement. Built from the roadway without toe access. Empirical design: Musser and Denning (2005); review: FHWA (2012).

figures.caption: Generic cross-section of a shored MSE (SMSE) wall system for steep terrains
figures.description: Shored MSE Walls for Steep Terrains and Low Volume Roads Applies to MSE walls for widening low volume roads in steep terrain with limited excavation. MSE reinforcement minimum length greater than 8 ft or 70% of wall height. Shoring usually soil nail walls; permanent shoring reduces long-term pressure on the MSE wall. Guidance: FHWA (2006) and GEC 11.

figures.caption: Minimum recommended geometry of a stable feature MSE (SFMSE) wall system
figures.description: Stable Feature (SFMSE) MSE Walls Applies to MSE walls constructed close in front of rock faces or other stable features. SFMSE walls are built in front of stable features such as rock faces. Behavior may resemble SMSE walls depending on the gap; guidance in GEC 11.

figures.caption: Shoot-in nail installation
figures.description: Shoot-In Nails Applies to temporary nail walls, landslide repairs and widening using launched nails. Launch speed over 200 mph at pressures approaching 2,500 psi. Bars typically 1-1/2 in. diameter, up to 20 ft long. Act as dowels (shear and bending), not as drilled and grouted nails. Proprietary; lacks simple comprehensive design procedures.

figures.caption: Screw-in nail installation
figures.description: Screw-In Nails Applies to helical nail stabilization at small or hard-to-access sites. Shaft typically 1.5-in. square solid steel; helix spacing about 3.6 times helix diameter. Acts as an anchor by helix bearing, not by grout bond. Corrosion is the major concern because coatings are damaged during installation.
